questions.question: A leader says: "You own the migration call — decide and let me know, but run the final answer past me before you announce it." What authority level has actually been granted?
options: Level 2, decide and inform, with a courtesy notification
Level 4, recommend and the leader decides, described as level 2
Level 3, decide after named consultation
Level 1, since the leader is only asking to be kept informed
questions.explanation: A required pre-announcement check is a veto point, which makes the call the leader's. A is the tempting answer because the sentence sounds like level 2 and is meant kindly. But the person will discover the real level only when they are overruled, and a person told level 4 honestly does better work than one corrected repeatedly at level 2.

questions.question: A PM meets the stated evidence standard in full and chooses the option the leader dislikes. What is the honest response?
options: Add the missing analysis the leader now realizes was needed, then re-decide together
Let it stand, or overrule openly and say so — but do not retroactively declare the process insufficient
Accept the decision but reduce the PM's level in this class immediately
Ask the PM to socialize the decision more widely before it takes effect
questions.explanation: The standard exists so that disagreement after it is met is about judgment, not process. A is the tempting distractor and the phase's recurring trap: it sounds collaborative and rigorous, but "re-decide together" after the standard was met takes the decision back while appearing to support it. Overruling is legitimate; disguising it is not.

questions.question: Which movement rule best grows judgment rather than compliance?
options: Move up after two quarters in the role with no major incidents
Move up when the leader feels comfortable that the person 'gets it'
Move up when the last three decisions in the class carried predictions written in advance and outcomes fell inside the stated confidence
Move up when the person's last three decisions turned out to be correct
questions.explanation: C rewards calibration — honest uncertainty that proves honest. D is the answer a competent PM gives, and it is close, but being right is partly luck and it quietly punishes anyone who states uncertainty. Someone right 90% of the time who always claims certainty is worse calibrated than someone right 70% who said 70%.

questions.question: A PM will hold authority over a build choice whose maintenance cost lands entirely on engineering, and the PM has no way to observe that cost. What is the right move?
options: Grant the authority anyway; ownership is how people learn
Split the decision so engineering decides the technical half and the PM decides scope
Place the PM at level 3 with the engineer who carries the cost, or change what the PM can see before granting it
Grant it, and review the outcome in six months
questions.explanation: Authority without visible consequence builds an uncorrected habit, because the feedback lands on someone else. B is tempting and often sensible elsewhere, but here it dodges the actual problem — the PM still cannot see the cost of the half they keep. Fix the visibility or name the consultation.

questions.question: A decision-rights map was written when a migration had not started and was cheap to reverse. Work is now three weeks in. What does the map most need?
options: A stated expiry condition, because the class has become one-way
A wider set of consulted people, since more is now at stake
Nothing — the rights were correctly assigned at the time
A shift of consequence ownership to the person doing the work
questions.explanation: Rights are written against a situation, and reversibility is part of that situation. Once the work is committed, the decision class changed and the row should have voided. C is tempting because the original assignment genuinely was correct; the failure is that nothing told anyone when it stopped being correct.
